html:
The Battle of Leuthen was fought on 5 December 1757 at Leuthen, now Lutynia in southwest Poland, in the province of Silesia. Frederick the Great of Prussia, with about 33,000 men, beat an Austrian army about twice that size under Prince Charles of Lorraine.

Frederick had seized rich Silesia from Austria in 1740, and the Seven Years' War was in large part Empress Maria Theresa's attempt to take it back. While he was away winning at Rossbach, the Austrians recaptured most of the province and its capital, Breslau. He marched back in two weeks. The Austrian line was about 7 km long. Frederick made a show of attacking its right, then marched his army out of sight behind low hills and fell on its left end. The Austrians tried to turn and form a new line around Leuthen village, but they were crushed together and driven off by evening. They lost about 22,000 men, more than half as prisoners. Prussia lost about 6,000.

Breslau surrendered two weeks later with 17,000 more men, and Prussia kept Silesia in the peace of 1763. Leuthen is seen as Frederick's finest battle. Napoleon called it a masterpiece of movement and resolve.
